# Round 6 (2026-09-22): unique + affordable + resume-worthy

Nick: "spitball more unique, affordable, good ideas that look good on a resume." All new (none
repeat rounds 1–5). Each has a resume line written out, because the resume line is the actual
deliverable being optimized here.

**Cheap parts worth knowing about (these unlock most of the list):**
- **VL53L0X time-of-flight laser rangefinder, ~$2–4.** mm-accurate, no ultrasonic flakiness.
- **RCWL-0516 doppler microwave motion, ~$1.** Sees *through* drywall/doors, unlike PIR.
- **QMC/HMC5883L 3-axis magnetometer, ~$1.50.** Detects steel vehicles; also senses AC current
  *without contact*.
- **Piezo disc, ~$0.50.** A contact microphone / structure-borne vibration pickup.
- **9 V AC-AC wall adapter, ~$8** (isolated, low-voltage — the only safe way near mains).

## A. Power-quality + grid-frequency monitor  ★ top pick
- **Hook:** the North American grid runs at 60.000 Hz, and the deviation is a live readout of
  generation-vs-load imbalance. Your building's *voltage* tells a different story than the
  grid's *frequency* — and separating them answers "was that flicker us or the utility?"
- **Sensors (~$12):** 9 V AC-AC adapter → (1) zero-crossing detector → GPIO interrupt, and
  (2) divided waveform → MCP3008 for RMS voltage. Add DS18B20 for the load/temperature story.
- **Cooperation, and it's a genuine diagnosis:** frequency deviation is grid-wide and identical
  for every customer; a voltage sag with *no* frequency excursion is local — your building, your
  panel, your neighbor's A/C compressor starting. One sensor can't tell those apart. A threshold
  definitely can't.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** and **C**, and here they're not decoration — *the interrupt-timestamp
  jitter is literally the measurement noise floor.* To resolve millihertz you must characterize
  and then minimize IRQ latency: SCHED_FIFO, IRQ affinity, interrupt vs. polled vs. kernel
  timestamping, measured three ways. Plus **D**.
- **Ground truth:** a $12 multimeter, and published grid-frequency data to sanity-check against.
  Induce sags with a space heater or a vacuum on the same circuit.
- **Resume line:** *"Built a power-quality monitor measuring mains frequency to ±X mHz; showed
  the Linux interrupt-timestamp jitter floor bounds the achievable resolution, and reduced it
  Y× with real-time scheduling and IRQ affinity. Distinguished building-local voltage sags from
  grid-wide frequency events."*
- **Safety, non-negotiable:** isolated AC-AC adapter only. Never touch mains, never open a panel.
- **Catch:** the "user" needs naming — a landlord whose tenants report flicker, a maker with
  equipment that resets, a lab with sensitive gear. Power quality is a real industry (Fluke
  sells $2k analyzers).

## B. Non-intrusive water-use disaggregation (read the meter you already have)
- **Hook:** most water meters have a magnet or reflective dial that ticks once per unit. Read it
  optically/magnetically and you get whole-house flow without a plumber — then *disaggregate* it.
- **Sensors (~$4):** hall sensor or IR reflective sensor on the meter (GPIO edge per tick) +
  DS18B20 on the hot line (hot vs cold draw) + optional second temp probe.
- **Cooperation:** flow rate alone is ambiguous. Flow *signature* (rate, duration, rise/fall
  shape) + hot-line temperature response classifies the fixture: toilet (sharp on, 45 s, cold
  only), shower (8 min, steady, hot), dishwasher (periodic bursts), irrigation (long, cold), and
  **a leak (continuous low flow that never stops — the thing that costs $400 and gets noticed on
  a bill two months later).**
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (tick interrupts, the polling comparison), **D** (months of history,
  crash-consistent), **E**.
- **Ground truth:** flush the toilet, run the shower, time it with a stopwatch. Trivially
  repeatable, labeled in an afternoon.
- **Resume line:** *"Non-intrusive load monitoring for water: classified five fixture types from
  flow signatures with X% accuracy against hand-logged ground truth, and detected continuous-flow
  leaks within N minutes."*
- **Catch:** meter must be accessible and have a readable marker; check first. (Flume sells
  exactly this for $200.)

## C. Doorway people counter (the Density.io problem)
- **Hook:** occupancy analytics is a real, funded industry (Density is a ~$1B company doing this
  with ToF sensors). Cameras are banned in most of the spaces that want it. You can build the
  camera-less version for $8.
- **Sensors (~$8):** two VL53L0X time-of-flight sensors across a doorway (which one breaks first
  = direction) + PIR or RCWL for presence corroboration.
- **Cooperation:** direction from two-sensor ordering; range distinguishes a person from a bag or
  a door swinging; presence sensor catches the tailgating case where two people cross together.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** is forced (direction depends on sub-millisecond edge ordering — the
  cleanest interrupt-vs-polling experiment on any list), **C**, **D** with a query CLI.
- **Ground truth:** stand there with a clicker for an hour. Honest, and the confusion matrix
  writes itself.
- **Resume line:** *"Built a camera-free bidirectional people counter: ±X% cumulative count error
  over N hours vs. hand-tallied ground truth, with measured event latency under CPU contention."*
- **Catch:** tailgating and doorway geometry are the real difficulty — narrow the claim to a
  standard-width door.

## D. Structure-borne footstep classifier (fall detection without a camera or a wearable)
- **Hook:** footsteps couple into the floor. A $0.50 piezo disc taped to the floor joist picks up
  walking, running, a dropped object, and a fall — through the structure, in the dark, with
  nothing worn and nothing recorded. This is an actual research area, and it's a strictly better
  answer to the professor's Seed 1 than a PIR.
- **Sensors (~$6):** piezo disc → MCP3008 (kHz sampling) + PIR or RCWL for room context.
- **Cooperation:** vibration says *what kind of impact*; the motion sensor says *whether someone
  is moving afterward.* "Large impact, then no motion for 60 s" is the event that matters — and
  it is unreachable by either sensor alone. That single sentence is the whole memo.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (kHz sampling, no drops, impulses are short), **C**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** drop a backpack, drop a watermelon, walk, run, jump. Fully inducible, and you
  can build a labeled library in one evening.
- **Resume line:** *"Classified structure-borne floor vibration into 4 event classes at kHz
  sampling with zero dropped samples under load; detected fall-shaped impact-then-stillness
  events with measured true/false-positive rates."*
- **Catch:** every floor is different (joists, carpet, slab) — the claim is "on this floor, after
  this calibration," and say so.

## E. Neighborhood traffic study (speed + volume, for an actual petition)
- **Hook:** traffic-calming petitions require *data* the city will accept, and residents don't
  have it. Two magnetometers spaced a known distance apart detect passing steel and give speed —
  this is how inductive loops work, minus the pavement saw.
- **Sensors (~$4):** 2× QMC5883L magnetometer, ~1–3 m apart, + a photoresistor/RTC for day-night.
- **Cooperation:** cross-correlate the two magnetic disturbance traces; the lag gives speed, the
  waveform's shape and amplitude give a crude size class (sedan vs truck).
- **Mechanisms:** **F/C** (correlation needs tight, known inter-sample timing — jitter becomes
  speed error directly, which is a beautiful justification sentence), **D**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** a stopwatch over a measured distance, or a friend driving past at a known
  speedometer reading.
- **Resume line:** *"Vehicle speed estimation by magnetic-signature cross-correlation: ±X mph vs.
  stopwatch ground truth; showed sampling jitter maps directly onto speed error and bounded it
  with real-time scheduling."*
- **Catch:** outdoor power and weatherproofing; keep sensors on private property at the curb.

## F. Acoustic pipe-leak localization (TDOA on a pipe)
- **Hook:** water utilities localize buried leaks by listening at two points and comparing
  arrival times. Sound moves ~4,700 m/s in copper, so the whole game is timestamp precision —
  which is an operating-systems problem wearing a plumbing costume.
- **Sensors (~$5):** 2× piezo contact discs clamped to a pipe at a known separation → MCP3008.
- **Cooperation:** neither sensor alone localizes anything; the *time difference of arrival*
  between them is the entire measurement.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** + **C**, hard-forced. Also the most honest demonstration of why sampling
  jitter is a physical error.
- **Ground truth:** tap the pipe at a measured position; the answer is a tape measure.
- **Resume line:** *"Time-difference-of-arrival localization on a pipe: located impacts to within
  X cm, bounded by the sampling-clock jitter I characterized."*
- **Catch:** the most technically ambitious on this list — MCP3008 sampling rate may force you to
  narrow from "localize to 10 cm" down to "identify which end," which is a legitimate narrowing
  but decide it early.

## G. Server-closet / lab thermal stratification map
- **Hook:** a campus lab or startup closet with a rack; the A/C is sized for the room, not the
  hot aisle. 6 temperature probes on **one 1-Wire bus** map the gradient.
- **Sensors (~$10):** 6× DS18B20 on a single bus + a vibration/current proxy for when the A/C is
  actually running.
- **Cooperation:** the gradient *between* probes is the signal (a single probe at the thermostat
  is exactly why the problem exists); A/C state says whether a hot spot is a cooling failure or a
  load spike.
- **Mechanisms:** **A** is the natural centerpiece — write your own 1-Wire character driver for
  a *multi-drop bus*, which forces real concurrent-access design (the spec's exact phrasing:
  "correct concurrent access; behavior under load"). Plus **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Wrote a Linux character driver for a 6-device 1-Wire bus with correct
  concurrent access under load; mapped a 9 °C stratification and correlated hot spots with
  compressor duty cycle."*
- **Catch:** needs a real room with a real owner — lab manager, IT staff, a startup.

## H. Non-contact appliance disaggregation by magnetic field
- **Hook:** current through a wire makes a field. A $1.50 magnetometer strapped to a breaker
  panel's exterior or an appliance cord senses *which* circuits are live — no clamp, no contact,
  nothing touching a conductor.
- **Sensors (~$4):** 2× magnetometer at different panel locations + DS18B20.
- **Cooperation:** two positions give crude source separation (which circuit region); the
  amplitude pattern plus on/off timing signatures identify appliances; temperature distinguishes
  heating loads.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (magnetometer at its max rate), **C**, **D**.
- **Resume line:** *"Non-contact appliance disaggregation from magnetic-field signatures:
  identified N appliances with X% accuracy without any electrical connection."*
- **Catch:** field strength falls off fast and panels are steel — validate placement in week one
  before committing. Higher technical risk than A/B/C above.

## I. Lightning / storm-front lead-time monitor
- **Hook:** the question isn't "is it raining," it's "how many minutes do I have?" — for a
  field crew, a rooftop, a livestock owner, a race director.
- **Sensors (~$12):** AS3935 lightning sensor (~$8, detects sferics up to ~40 km) + BMP280
  pressure + DHT22.
- **Cooperation:** strike rate and estimated distance give approach; pressure-drop *rate* and
  humidity give front arrival. Together: a lead-time estimate. Either alone: a number.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (strikes are asynchronous interrupts), **D**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** National Weather Service alerts and radar timestamps — a free, official
  reference you can score yourself against, which is rare and looks excellent in a report.
- **Resume line:** *"Storm lead-time estimator scored against NWS alert timestamps: median X
  minutes of advance warning over N storms."*
- **Catch:** Colorado's storm season is thin by November; the AS3935 has notorious false triggers
  from motors and fluorescent lights (the false-positive work *is* the project).

## J. Cosmic-ray muon flux vs. barometric pressure  (the "wait, what?" project)
- **Hook:** muon flux at sea level is measurably anticorrelated with barometric pressure (~−0.2%
  per hPa) because a denser atmosphere absorbs more. You can measure a real particle-physics
  coefficient on a Raspberry Pi in a dorm room.
- **Sensors (~$35):** Geiger tube kit (~$30, pulse output → GPIO) + BMP280 (~$2).
- **Cooperation:** the count rate alone is meaningless noise; *correlated against pressure over
  days* it produces a physical constant you can compare against published values.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (random-arrival pulse counting — Poisson statistics, and the polling
  comparison is stark), **D** (weeks of counts must survive power cuts).
- **Resume line:** *"Measured the barometric coefficient of cosmic-ray muon flux (−X%/hPa,
  vs. −0.2%/hPa published) from 3 weeks of interrupt-counted detections."*
- **Catch:** **the most expensive idea here (~$35 in sensors)** and the weakest "user" — the
  honest user is a physics teacher who wants a classroom demo. Statistics need weeks, so it must
  start at M2. Include it only if the uniqueness is worth the user-story fight.

## K. Doppler-vs-PIR through-wall occupancy
- **Hook:** RCWL-0516 doppler sees through drywall; PIR does not. Their *disagreement* is
  information — "motion in the next room," "someone present but still" (PIR misses stillness,
  doppler catches breathing-scale motion at close range).
- **Sensors (~$4):** RCWL-0516 + PIR + DS18B20.
- **Cooperation:** a 2×2 truth table across both sensors maps to four states (empty / present-
  still / present-moving / adjacent-room), which is exactly the "an if-statement couldn't do
  this" requirement.
- **Mechanisms:** **B**, **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Sensor-fusion occupancy state machine resolving 4 states from two motion
  sensors with complementary failure modes; X% accuracy vs. logged ground truth."*
- **Catch:** RCWL-0516 is famously twitchy (it triggers on rain, fans, and itself) — taming it is
  the actual engineering, so say so in the memo rather than discovering it in week 9.

## L. Queue-length monitor for a café / dining hall / lab printer
- **Hook:** "is the line long right now, and when is it usually short?" — a past-tense and
  predictive question. The user is the manager who staffs the counter.
- **Sensors (~$7):** 2× VL53L0X (line depth at two points) + RCWL or PIR.
- **Cooperation:** range says how far the line extends; the second sensor plus dwell-time gives
  throughput (people served per minute), so you can report *wait time*, not just length.
- **Mechanisms:** **D** + query CLI, **E**, **B**.
- **Resume line:** *"Queue-length and wait-time estimator: predicted wait within ±X min vs.
  stopwatch ground truth across N hours."*
- **Catch:** needs permission from a business; a campus lab printer or a club room is the
  low-friction version.

## M. Gas-stove CO and combustion-safety monitor
- **Hook:** a poorly burning gas stove or furnace produces CO; cheap CO sensors exist but drift
  badly, so the honest engineering is compensating for a bad sensor — which is the professor's
  §5 doctrine made literal.
- **Sensors (~$6):** MQ-7 CO (~$3, needs ADC + a heater duty cycle) + DHT22 + reed on the
  kitchen window.
- **Cooperation:** MQ sensors respond to humidity and temperature as much as to CO, so the
  compensation *requires* the second sensor; window state explains ventilation.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (the MQ-7 requires a precisely timed 60 s/90 s heater cycle — a real
  deadline, and a gorgeous SCHED_FIFO justification), **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Temperature/humidity-compensated CO monitoring on an uncalibrated $3 sensor,
  with a real-time heater duty cycle holding ±X ms timing under load."*
- **Catch:** never claim life-safety. The claim is "detects elevated CO relative to its own
  baseline," and the limitations section says loudly that this is not a certified CO alarm.

## Ranking for "unique + affordable + resume"
1. **A. Power-quality / grid-frequency monitor** — most unique, the OS mechanism *is* the
   measurement, ~$12, real industry. Best story of anything in this file.
2. **D. Structure-borne footstep/fall classifier** — research-grade idea, $6, inducible ground
   truth in an evening, beats Seed 1 at its own problem.
3. **C. Doorway people counter** — a literal funded-startup product category, forced mechanism B,
   ground truth is a clicker.
4. **B. Water disaggregation** — best "saved someone money" story; NILM is a term that lands.
5. **G. Thermal stratification + 1-Wire driver** — if the goal is "wrote a Linux kernel driver"
   on the resume, this is the cleanest path to it.

- **Catch:** the most technically ambitious on this list — MCP3008 sampling rate may force you to
  narrow from "localize to 10 cm" down to "identify which end," which is a legitimate narrowing
  but decide it early.

## G. Server-closet / lab thermal stratification map
- **Hook:** a campus lab or startup closet with a rack; the A/C is sized for the room, not the
  hot aisle. 6 temperature probes on **one 1-Wire bus** map the gradient.
- **Sensors (~$10):** 6× DS18B20 on a single bus + a vibration/current proxy for when the A/C is
  actually running.
- **Cooperation:** the gradient *between* probes is the signal (a single probe at the thermostat
  is exactly why the problem exists); A/C state says whether a hot spot is a cooling failure or a
  load spike.
- **Mechanisms:** **A** is the natural centerpiece — write your own 1-Wire character driver for
  a *multi-drop bus*, which forces real concurrent-access design (the spec's exact phrasing:
  "correct concurrent access; behavior under load"). Plus **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Wrote a Linux character driver for a 6-device 1-Wire bus with correct
  concurrent access under load; mapped a 9 °C stratification and correlated hot spots with
  compressor duty cycle."*
- **Catch:** needs a real room with a real owner — lab manager, IT staff, a startup.

## H. Non-contact appliance disaggregation by magnetic field
- **Hook:** current through a wire makes a field. A $1.50 magnetometer strapped to a breaker
  panel's exterior or an appliance cord senses *which* circuits are live — no clamp, no contact,
  nothing touching a conductor.
- **Sensors (~$4):** 2× magnetometer at different panel locations + DS18B20.
- **Cooperation:** two positions give crude source separation (which circuit region); the
  amplitude pattern plus on/off timing signatures identify appliances; temperature distinguishes
  heating loads.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (magnetometer at its max rate), **C**, **D**.
- **Resume line:** *"Non-contact appliance disaggregation from magnetic-field signatures:
  identified N appliances with X% accuracy without any electrical connection."*
- **Catch:** field strength falls off fast and panels are steel — validate placement in week one
  before committing. Higher technical risk than A/B/C above.

## I. Lightning / storm-front lead-time monitor
- **Hook:** the question isn't "is it raining," it's "how many minutes do I have?" — for a
  field crew, a rooftop, a livestock owner, a race director.
- **Sensors (~$12):** AS3935 lightning sensor (~$8, detects sferics up to ~40 km) + BMP280
  pressure + DHT22.
- **Cooperation:** strike rate and estimated distance give approach; pressure-drop *rate* and
  humidity give front arrival. Together: a lead-time estimate. Either alone: a number.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (strikes are asynchronous interrupts), **D**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** National Weather Service alerts and radar timestamps — a free, official
  reference you can score yourself against, which is rare and looks excellent in a report.
- **Resume line:** *"Storm lead-time estimator scored against NWS alert timestamps: median X
  minutes of advance warning over N storms."*
- **Catch:** Colorado's storm season is thin by November; the AS3935 has notorious false triggers
  from motors and fluorescent lights (the false-positive work *is* the project).

## J. Cosmic-ray muon flux vs. barometric pressure  (the "wait, what?" project)
- **Hook:** muon flux at sea level is measurably anticorrelated with barometric pressure (~−0.2%
  per hPa) because a denser atmosphere absorbs more. You can measure a real particle-physics
  coefficient on a Raspberry Pi in a dorm room.
- **Sensors (~$35):** Geiger tube kit (~$30, pulse output → GPIO) + BMP280 (~$2).
- **Cooperation:** the count rate alone is meaningless noise; *correlated against pressure over
  days* it produces a physical constant you can compare against published values.
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (random-arrival pulse counting — Poisson statistics, and the polling
  comparison is stark), **D** (weeks of counts must survive power cuts).
- **Resume line:** *"Measured the barometric coefficient of cosmic-ray muon flux (−X%/hPa,
  vs. −0.2%/hPa published) from 3 weeks of interrupt-counted detections."*
- **Catch:** **the most expensive idea here (~$35 in sensors)** and the weakest "user" — the
  honest user is a physics teacher who wants a classroom demo. Statistics need weeks, so it must
  start at M2. Include it only if the uniqueness is worth the user-story fight.

## K. Doppler-vs-PIR through-wall occupancy
- **Hook:** RCWL-0516 doppler sees through drywall; PIR does not. Their *disagreement* is
  information — "motion in the next room," "someone present but still" (PIR misses stillness,
  doppler catches breathing-scale motion at close range).
- **Sensors (~$4):** RCWL-0516 + PIR + DS18B20.
- **Cooperation:** a 2×2 truth table across both sensors maps to four states (empty / present-
  still / present-moving / adjacent-room), which is exactly the "an if-statement couldn't do
  this" requirement.
- **Mechanisms:** **B**, **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Sensor-fusion occupancy state machine resolving 4 states from two motion
  sensors with complementary failure modes; X% accuracy vs. logged ground truth."*
- **Catch:** RCWL-0516 is famously twitchy (it triggers on rain, fans, and itself) — taming it is
  the actual engineering, so say so in the memo rather than discovering it in week 9.

## L. Queue-length monitor for a café / dining hall / lab printer
- **Hook:** "is the line long right now, and when is it usually short?" — a past-tense and
  predictive question. The user is the manager who staffs the counter.
- **Sensors (~$7):** 2× VL53L0X (line depth at two points) + RCWL or PIR.
- **Cooperation:** range says how far the line extends; the second sensor plus dwell-time gives
  throughput (people served per minute), so you can report *wait time*, not just length.
- **Mechanisms:** **D** + query CLI, **E**, **B**.
- **Resume line:** *"Queue-length and wait-time estimator: predicted wait within ±X min vs.
  stopwatch ground truth across N hours."*
- **Catch:** needs permission from a business; a campus lab printer or a club room is the
  low-friction version.

## M. Gas-stove CO and combustion-safety monitor
- **Hook:** a poorly burning gas stove or furnace produces CO; cheap CO sensors exist but drift
  badly, so the honest engineering is compensating for a bad sensor — which is the professor's
  §5 doctrine made literal.
- **Sensors (~$6):** MQ-7 CO (~$3, needs ADC + a heater duty cycle) + DHT22 + reed on the
  kitchen window.
- **Cooperation:** MQ sensors respond to humidity and temperature as much as to CO, so the
  compensation *requires* the second sensor; window state explains ventilation.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (the MQ-7 requires a precisely timed 60 s/90 s heater cycle — a real
  deadline, and a gorgeous SCHED_FIFO justification), **D**, **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Temperature/humidity-compensated CO monitoring on an uncalibrated $3 sensor,
  with a real-time heater duty cycle holding ±X ms timing under load."*
- **Catch:** never claim life-safety. The claim is "detects elevated CO relative to its own
  baseline," and the limitations section says loudly that this is not a certified CO alarm.

1. **A. Power-quality / grid-frequency monitor** — most unique, the OS mechanism *is* the
   measurement, ~$12, real industry. Best story of anything in this file.
2. **D. Structure-borne footstep/fall classifier** — research-grade idea, $6, inducible ground

3. **C. Doorway people counter** — a literal funded-startup product category, forced mechanism B,

4. **B. Water disaggregation** — best "saved someone money" story; NILM is a term that lands.
5. **G. Thermal stratification + 1-Wire driver** — if the goal is "wrote a Linux kernel driver"
   on the resume, this is the cleanest path to it.

- **VL53L0X time-of-flight laser rangefinder, ~$2–4** — millimeter-accurate, none of the ultrasonic flakiness
- **RCWL-0516 doppler motion, ~$1** — sees *through* drywall and doors, unlike PIR
- **QMC5883L magnetometer, ~$1.50** — detects steel vehicles, and senses AC current without contact
- **Piezo disc, ~$0.50** — a contact microphone for structure-borne vibration
- **9 V AC-AC wall adapter, ~$8** — isolated, low-voltage, the only safe way to go near mains

## A. Power-quality + grid-frequency monitor ★

The grid runs at 60.000 Hz and the deviation is a live readout of generation-vs-load imbalance. Your building's *voltage* tells a different story than the grid's *frequency*, and separating them answers "was that flicker us or the utility?"

Sensors (~$12): AC-AC adapter → zero-crossing detector on a GPIO interrupt, plus the divided waveform into an ADC for RMS voltage. Cooperation is a real diagnosis: frequency deviation is grid-wide and identical for every customer, so a voltage sag with *no* frequency excursion is local — your panel, your neighbor's A/C compressor starting.

Here's why it's the best fit for this course: **the interrupt-timestamp jitter is literally the measurement noise floor.** To resolve millihertz you have to characterize and then minimize IRQ latency — real-time scheduling, IRQ affinity, interrupt vs. polled vs. kernel timestamping, measured three ways. Mechanisms B and C aren't decoration, they're the instrument.

> *"Built a power-quality monitor measuring mains frequency to ±X mHz; showed the Linux interrupt-timestamp jitter floor bounds achievable resolution and reduced it Y× with real-time scheduling and IRQ affinity."*

Safety: isolated AC-AC adapter only, never touch mains or open a panel. Catch: you need to name a user — a landlord whose tenants report flicker, a maker whose equipment resets.

## B. Non-intrusive water-use disaggregation

Most water meters have a magnet or reflective dial that ticks once per unit. Read it, then *disaggregate* it. Sensors (~$4): hall or IR sensor on the meter + a temp probe on the hot line.

Flow rate alone is ambiguous; flow *signature* plus hot-line temperature response classifies the fixture — toilet (sharp on, 45 s, cold), shower (8 min, steady, hot), dishwasher (periodic bursts), irrigation, and the one that matters: a continuous low flow that never stops, the leak that costs $400 and gets noticed on a bill two months later. Ground truth is a stopwatch and a toilet handle.

> *"Non-intrusive load monitoring for water: classified five fixture types from flow signatures with X% accuracy, detected continuous-flow leaks within N minutes."*

## C. Doorway people counter

Occupancy analytics is a funded industry — Density is a ~$1B company doing exactly this with ToF sensors, because cameras are banned in most spaces that want the data. You can build it for $8: two VL53L0X across a doorway (which breaks first = direction) + a presence sensor for tailgating.

**B is forced** — direction depends on sub-millisecond ordering of two edges, which is the cleanest interrupt-vs-polling experiment on any list I've given you. Ground truth: stand there with a clicker for an hour.

> *"Camera-free bidirectional people counter: ±X% cumulative count error over N hours vs. hand-tallied ground truth, with measured event latency under CPU contention."*

## D. Structure-borne footstep classifier

Footsteps couple into the floor. A $0.50 piezo taped to a joist picks up walking, running, a dropped object, and a fall — through the structure, in the dark, nothing worn, nothing recorded. It's an active research area and a strictly better answer to the professor's Seed 1 than a PIR.

Sensors (~$6): piezo → ADC at kHz + a motion sensor for context. The fusion sentence is the whole memo: vibration says *what kind of impact*, motion says *whether anyone moved afterward* — "large impact, then no motion for 60 seconds" is unreachable by either sensor alone. Mechanism F is forced (impulses are short, a dropped sample loses the event). Ground truth in one evening: drop a backpack, drop a watermelon, walk, run, jump.

> *"Classified structure-borne floor vibration into 4 event classes at kHz sampling with zero dropped samples under load; detected fall-shaped impact-then-stillness events with measured true/false-positive rates."*

## E. Neighborhood traffic study

Traffic-calming petitions require data the city accepts, and residents don't have it. Two magnetometers a known distance apart detect passing steel; cross-correlating the traces gives speed. That's how inductive loops work, minus the pavement saw. ~$4.

Sampling jitter maps *directly* onto speed error, which makes the real-time-scheduling justification write itself. Ground truth: a stopwatch, or a friend driving at a known speedometer reading.

> *"Vehicle speed estimation by magnetic-signature cross-correlation: ±X mph vs. stopwatch ground truth; bounded jitter-induced error with real-time scheduling."*

## F. Acoustic pipe-leak localization

Water utilities localize buried leaks by listening at two points and comparing arrival times. Sound moves ~4,700 m/s in copper, so the entire game is timestamp precision — an OS problem in a plumbing costume. Two piezo discs on a pipe, ~$5. Ground truth is a tape measure: tap the pipe at a measured spot.

> *"Time-difference-of-arrival localization on a pipe: located impacts to within X cm, bounded by the sampling-clock jitter I characterized."*

Most technically ambitious here — the ADC's rate may force you to narrow from "localize to 10 cm" to "identify which end." Legitimate narrowing, but decide it early.

## G. Server-closet thermal stratification map

> *"Wrote a Linux character driver for a 6-device 1-Wire bus with correct concurrent access under load; mapped a 9 °C stratification and correlated hot spots with compressor duty cycle."*

## H. Non-contact appliance disaggregation

A $1.50 magnetometer on the *outside* of a breaker panel senses which circuits are live — no clamp, no contact, nothing touching a conductor. Two positions give crude source separation. Higher risk than the others: field strength falls off fast and panels are steel, so validate placement in week one.

> *"Non-contact appliance disaggregation from magnetic-field signatures: identified N appliances with X% accuracy without any electrical connection."*

## J. Cosmic-ray muon flux vs. barometric pressure

# Round 7 (2026-09-22): the "chicken coop door" shape — actuated discrimination devices

Nick pointed at a project from last year: a chicken coop door that **opens only if it's a
chicken.** He wants that flavor, but resume-grade. Naming the pattern, because it's generative:

**actuator + discrimination problem + asymmetric failure costs + one-sentence pitch + no camera.**
The commercial version costs $150 and cheats with an RFID chip; ours discriminates from cheap
sensors and real signal processing.

**Why this shape fits the rubric unusually well:**
- **C is forced honestly.** "Decide in 400 ms while the animal is at the threshold" is a latency
  budget you must *meet*, not admire (the professor's own phrasing in Seed 3). Deadline-miss rate
  becomes a headline metric instead of a contrived one.
- **The failure-mode table writes itself.** Servo jams, door closes on an animal, power dies
  mid-cycle, sensor unplugged with the door open. Needs position feedback or current-sense as a
  safety interlock — real engineering, and exactly what §8 asks for.
- **Fault injection is theatrical.** Unplug the sensor mid-demo and the correct behavior is
  "fail safe to open, log it, tell the user" — a designed decision you can defend.
- **Asymmetric error costs force a real analysis discussion.** A false-open (raccoon gets in) and
  a false-close (hen locked out) are not equally bad, so you tune an operating point, not an
  accuracy number. ROC-curve reasoning in a sophomore project looks excellent.
- **RFID/microchip = an if-statement = fails §3.3.** Tag-free discrimination is the project.

## 1. Gait-and-mass pet door — "knows your cat from the neighbor's cat"  ★ top pick
- **Pitch:** the $150 microchip cat flap requires a chip on the collar. Ours identifies the animal
  by *how it walks*.
- **Sensors (~$9):** load cell + HX711 under an approach mat, sampled **fast** (80 Hz+) so a
  1-second walk-across becomes a pressure *time series*, not a weight; plus 2× VL53L0X ToF across
  the flap for height profile and direction. Servo or solenoid latch (~$3).
- **Discrimination:** step cadence, stride interval, peak-per-step distribution, total mass, body
  length and height from ToF. Your 4.5 kg cat, the neighbor's 4.4 kg cat, and a raccoon are
  separable by *gait*, not by weight. This is real research territory (floor-pressure gait
  recognition) done with $9 of parts.
- **Cooperation:** mass/gait says *who*; ToF says *how big and which direction* (and catches the
  tailgating raccoon following the cat in).
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (the walk-across is a short high-rate capture where a dropped sample
  corrupts the gait vector), **C** (unlock before the animal reaches the flap), **E** (a
  supervisor must never leave the latch stuck — a trapped pet is the nightmare scenario).
- **Ground truth:** your cat, a friend's cat, a stuffed animal dragged across on a string, a
  weighted box. Dozens of labeled walk-throughs per evening. Confusion matrix is easy.
- **Resume line:** *"Tag-free animal identification from floor-pressure gait signatures: X%
  accuracy distinguishing N animals, driving a door actuator within a 400 ms deadline with a
  measured deadline-miss rate under load."*
- **Catch:** needs an existing cat flap or a mockup frame, and a cooperative cat. The stuffed-
  animal-on-a-string trick covers the "second animal" you don't own.

## 2. Two-cat feeder — "only opens for the cat that's on the diet"
- **Pitch:** SureFeed sells this for $150 with a microchip. Multi-cat households where one cat is
  diabetic, on prescription food, or obese are extremely common, and the wrong cat eating the
  wrong food is a vet bill.
- **Sensors (~$8):** load cell under the approach platform (mass + gait, as above) + IR break-beam
  or ToF at the bowl opening. Servo-driven lid (~$3).
- **Cooperation:** platform weight identifies the cat; the beam confirms a head actually entered
  (a cat leaning over from outside the platform is the adversarial case and the fun part).
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (lid must open before the cat gives up and leaves — measure it), **D**
  (per-cat feeding history must survive a power cut), **E**.
- **Resume line:** *"Mass-and-gait animal discrimination driving a servo-actuated feeder: X%
  correct-cat accuracy with a measured false-open rate; per-animal intake logged across 48 h."*
- **Catch:** you need two animals with distinguishable masses — verify before committing.

## 3. Driveway gate that knows *your* car — magnetic signature
- **Pitch:** license-plate readers cost thousands. Every vehicle distorts the earth's magnetic
  field in a signature pattern set by its steel mass and layout. A $1.50 magnetometer reads it.
- **Sensors (~$6):** 2× QMC5883L magnetometer spaced along the approach (signature + speed from
  cross-correlation) + ToF or break-beam for presence confirmation. Relay/actuator to trigger the
  gate or just a lighted "recognized" indicator if there's no gate.
- **Discrimination:** template-match the magnetic waveform against learned signatures — your car,
  the roommate's, "unknown." Speed from the two-sensor lag rejects a bicycle or a pedestrian with
  a steel frame.
- **Mechanisms:** **F/C** (cross-correlation needs tight inter-sample timing — jitter converts
  directly into misclassification), **D**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** drive your own car past 30 times; borrow two friends' cars. Easy, labeled.
- **Resume line:** *"Vehicle identification by magnetic-signature template matching: X% accuracy
  across N vehicles at up to Y mph, with sampling jitter bounded by real-time scheduling."*
- **Catch:** needs a driveway and outdoor power. Works without an actual gate (indicator + log),
  which is the risk-free scoped-down version.

## 4. Deer sprinkler that doesn't spray the mail carrier
- **Pitch:** motion-activated sprinklers exist and they spray *everything* — the dog, the mail
  carrier, you. A garden deterrent that fires only at deer is a genuinely better product.
- **Sensors (~$8):** vertical pair (or small array) of VL53L0X / ultrasonic giving a **height
  profile** + RCWL doppler or PIR for motion, + piezo/vibration in the bed for browsing. Solenoid
  valve or servo on a hose (~$6).
- **Discrimination:** height profile (deer ~1.2 m at shoulder, human ~1.7 m, dog ~0.5 m) plus
  approach speed and dwell. A human walks through; a deer stops and lowers its head — and the
  *head-lowering* is a range change you can actually detect.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (a deer gives you ~2 s; a late spray teaches it nothing — measure the
  deadline miss rate), **B**, **E**.
- **Ground truth:** you, a friend, a dog, and a cardboard deer silhouette at measured heights.
  Fort Collins deer do the rest.
- **Resume line:** *"Height-profile and motion-fusion classifier driving a sprinkler actuator:
  X% deer detection with Y% false-trigger rate on humans/pets, decided within a 2 s window."*
- **Catch:** water + electronics outdoors; season and deer traffic vary. The indicator-light
  version proves the classifier without plumbing.

## 5. Raccoon-proof trash lid — "knows a raccoon from a roommate"
- **Pitch:** raccoons open trash cans; Fort Collins bear-and-raccoon rules make this a real
  municipal problem, and bear-proof cans cost $200+.
- **Sensors (~$7):** ToF pointed up the approach (human hand arrives at ~1 m, raccoon at ~0.2 m)
  + load/vibration sensor on the lid (an animal climbing on it vs. a hand lifting it) + light
  sensor for day/night prior. Servo latch (~$3).
- **Discrimination:** approach *height* + lid-force signature + time-of-day prior. "Downward
  force at ground level at 3 a.m." unlatches nothing; "approach at hand height" unlatches
  instantly.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (a human shouldn't wait — unlatch under ~300 ms), **B**, **E**, **D**.
- **Resume line:** *"Multi-sensor intruder discrimination driving a latch actuator: 100% human
  unlatch success over N trials with zero animal-triggered unlatches across a 48 h field run."*
- **Catch:** provoking raccoons on demand is the hard part; a weighted stuffed animal and a
  broomstick simulate the ground-level case, labeled as such.

## 6. Kitchen fan that knows steam from smoke
- **Pitch:** everyone's smoke alarm goes off when they shower or sear a steak, so everyone
  disables it — which is *why* people die in fires. A hood fan that fires only on real combustion
  products is a product with an obvious reason to exist.
- **Sensors (~$8):** cheap optical dust sensor (GP2Y1010, ~$4) + DHT22 + DS18B20 at the hood.
  Relay drives the fan (~$2).
- **Discrimination:** steam = humidity spike with **large** particles and a fast decay; smoke =
  particles with humidity *flat* and slow decay; burnt food = both, plus a temperature ramp. One
  sensor cannot separate these — this is the textbook "an if-statement couldn't do it" case.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** (the dust sensor needs a precisely timed ~0.32 ms LED pulse and sample —
  a genuine microsecond deadline that justifies SCHED_FIFO better than almost anything), **D**,
  **E**.
- **Ground truth:** boil a kettle, run a hot shower, burn toast, blow out a candle. Four labeled
  classes in one evening, repeatable forever.
- **Resume line:** *"Reduced nuisance ventilation triggers from X% to Y% by fusing particulate,

- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms, synchronization primitives (semaphores/locks/mutexes/condition variables — flagged as needed across *four consecutive lectures* now, to coordinate shared memory, thread data dependencies, and kernel module access — very likely next), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock, sockets/networking mechanics — standard OS-course territory not yet reached. ## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms, synchronization primitives (semaphores/locks/mutexes/condition variables — flagged as needed across *four consecutive lectures* now, to coordinate shared memory, thread data dependencies, and kernel module access — very likely next), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock, sockets/networking mechanics — standard OS-course territory not yet reached. # Round 8 (2026-09-22): unique for its own sake — "wait, you can measure that?"

Nick's clarification: the coop-door example was about **uniqueness**, not about the
discriminate-A-from-B category. (Also: the driveway gate was *magnetic* signature, not heat — a
$1.50 magnetometer reading how a car's steel distorts the earth's field. The thermal version
needs a ~$20 IR array and performs worse.)

**The generator used here:** *what invisible thing can a $3 sensor reveal that normally costs
hundreds or thousands to measure?* Four sub-patterns, so Nick can generate his own:
1. **Off-label sensor use** — a magnetometer reading cars, a photoresistor reading flicker.
2. **Hidden-variable inference** — measuring a decay curve to get a constant you can't sense
   directly (air-change rate, thermal time constant).
3. **Sensing through a medium** — structure, pipe, soil, mattress.
4. **Surprising scale** — microseconds, millihertz, single raindrops.

## 1. Sleep vitals from bed vibration (ballistocardiography)  ★ top pick
- **The trick:** every heartbeat moves your body slightly. A load cell under one mattress leg (or
  an accelerometer on the bed frame) picks up that motion *through the mattress.* Bandpass
  0.1–0.5 Hz → respiration. Bandpass 0.8–2.5 Hz → heart rate. This is a real clinical technique
  (ballistocardiography); Withings sells the consumer version for $130.
- **Sensors (~$8):** HX711 + load cell under a bed leg + DHT22 for room temperature/humidity.
- **Cooperation:** the vibration channel gives vitals and movement; the environment channel
  explains them (restlessness correlates with a room above ~22 °C, and you can *show* that over
  weeks). Also: presence detection — the bed knows when it's occupied, which gates everything.
- **Intelligence:** bandpass filtering, FFT/autocorrelation peak-picking, motion-artifact
  rejection, sleep-vs-wake segmentation. Nothing about this is a threshold.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (continuous sampling where a dropped window corrupts a beat estimate),
  **C**, **D** (a night's series must survive a power cut), **E**.
- **Ground truth:** a $15 fingertip pulse oximeter and a stopwatch for breaths. You can validate
  against a reference *in bed, tonight*, which almost no other idea offers.
- **Resume line:** *"Extracted respiration and heart rate from mattress-borne ballistocardiogram
  signals using a $5 load cell: X bpm mean absolute error vs. pulse-oximeter reference over N
  nights."*
- **Catch:** not a medical device — say so in the memo, the README and the limitations section.
  Signal quality depends on mattress type; a foam mattress may kill it, so test night one.

## 2. Light-flicker meter (IEEE 1789 bulb rating)
- **The trick:** cheap LED bulbs flicker at 100–120 Hz, and bad ones cause headaches, eye strain,
  and migraines. There's a real standard for it (IEEE 1789) with defined metrics — percent
  flicker and flicker index. Professional flicker meters cost $500+. A photodiode or LDR into a
  fast ADC measures it for $5.
- **Sensors (~$7):** photodiode/LDR + MCP3008 (sampled at kHz) + DS18B20 on the bulb housing.
- **Cooperation:** LED drivers get worse as they heat up, so flicker measured cold vs. at thermal
  equilibrium is a *different number* — the temperature channel is what turns a single reading
  into a real finding. Also catches dimmer-induced flicker.
- **Mechanisms:** **F** (you're sampling kHz waveforms — drops corrupt the spectrum), **C**
  (uniform sampling intervals are the measurement's validity), **D**.
- **Ground truth:** an incandescent bulb (known near-zero flicker at the filament's thermal
  inertia), a known-cheap LED, a dimmer at several settings. Fully controlled, indoors, any day.
- **Resume line:** *"Built a photometric flicker analyzer computing percent flicker and flicker
  index per IEEE 1789 at kHz sampling; rated N bulbs and identified M failing the standard's
  low-risk threshold."*
- **User:** a building manager, a professor with a migraine-prone student, a lab with
  photosensitive equipment, an apartment complex replacing fixtures.
- **Why it's unique:** nobody in a sophomore OS class has ever measured flicker. It sounds like it
  needs a lab instrument, and it needs an ADC and a scheduler instead.

## 3. Ultrasonic anemometer (wind speed *and* air temperature from microseconds)
- **The trick:** send an ultrasonic pulse upwind and downwind between two transducers. The
  *difference* in time-of-flight gives wind speed; the *sum* gives the speed of sound, which gives
  you air temperature — from the same two microsecond measurements. Commercial ultrasonic
  anemometers are $500+ and have no moving parts, which is why airports use them.
- **Sensors (~$6):** 2 ultrasonic transceivers facing each other (~50 cm apart) + a temp/humidity
  sensor as the cross-check.
- **Cooperation:** the reference thermometer *validates your derived* sonic temperature — one
  sensor checking a quantity the other computed, which is an unusually elegant cooperation story
  for the memo.
- **Mechanisms:** **C** and **F**, forced as hard as anywhere in this file — at 340 m/s over
  0.5 m, wind of 1 m/s shifts the flight time by ~4 µs, so **scheduling jitter converts directly
  into wind-speed error.** That single sentence justifies SCHED_FIFO better than any other
  project here.
- **Ground truth:** a $12 handheld anemometer, or a car window at a known speed on a calm day.
- **Resume line:** *"Ultrasonic anemometer from microsecond time-of-flight differentials: ±X m/s
  vs. reference, with sampling jitter characterized as the dominant error term and reduced Y× by
  real-time scheduling."*
- **Catch:** the most physics-forward idea here, and the hardest. Prove you can resolve the
  timing on a bench before committing; the fallback (fixed-distance speed-of-sound thermometry
  alone) still works.

## 4. Building envelope audit — thermal time constant and heat-loss coefficient
- **The trick:** when the heat shuts off, a room cools exponentially, and the time constant τ is a
  physical property of the building (the RC of the envelope). Combine it with when the furnace
  actually ran and you get a heat-loss coefficient — the number a $400 professional energy audit
  sells you.
- **Sensors (~$8):** indoor DS18B20 + outdoor DS18B20 + a vibration or magnetic sensor telling
  you when the furnace/heater is actually running.
- **Cooperation:** the temperature difference alone is meaningless without knowing whether heat
  was being added; the furnace-state channel is what turns two thermometers into an energy model.
- **Intelligence:** exponential decay fitting on every off-cycle, regression of duty cycle against
  outdoor temperature (this is real building science — the "energy signature" method), and
  detection of τ *changing* over weeks (a window left open, insulation settling).
- **Mechanisms:** **D** (weeks of history, crash-consistent), **E**, **A** (multi-drop 1-Wire
  driver if you add more probes).
- **Ground truth:** open a window on purpose and watch τ drop — a provoked, labeled, dramatic
  experiment you can run in an hour.
- **Resume line:** *"Passive building-envelope characterization: estimated thermal time constant
  and heat-loss coefficient from cooling-curve fits and furnace duty cycles; detected a 34% τ
  reduction from a single open window."*
- **User:** a renter deciding whether to complain, a landlord, a roommate group arguing about the
  gas bill.

## 5. Room air-change rate from CO2 decay (a $15 tracer-gas test)
- **The trick:** after people leave a room, CO2 decays exponentially toward outdoor levels, and
  the decay constant *is* the room's air changes per hour. Ventilation engineers measure this with
  tracer gases and equipment costing thousands. You measure it with a $12 sensor and a curve fit.
- **Sensors (~$16):** MH-Z19 CO2 + BME280 + a reed switch on the door (door state changes the
  answer completely, which is the point).
- **Cooperation:** the decay constant is only valid for a known door/window state, so the reed
  switch isn't a second data stream — it's the *validity condition* for the first one's analysis.
- **Mechanisms:** **E** (UART sensor in its own process — they hang), **D** + query CLI, **B**.
- **Ground truth:** breathe into the room to spike CO2, leave, and fit the decay. Repeat with the
  door open, the window open, the fan on. Four labeled conditions in an afternoon.
- **Resume line:** *"Measured room air-change rates (ACH) from CO2 decay-curve fits across N
  ventilation conditions, quantifying a Z× difference between closed-door and cracked-window
  states."*
- **Why it lands:** ACH is a metric people genuinely cared about post-2020, and "I built the cheap
  version of a tracer-gas test" is a sentence that gets a follow-up question.

## 6. One sensor, whole-house appliance census (structure-borne)
- **The trick:** every machine in a building couples vibration into the structure. A single
  accelerometer on a floor joist or wall stud hears the furnace, the washer, the dryer, the garage
  door, and footsteps — each with a distinct spectral fingerprint, all through the wood.
- **Sensors (~$6):** MPU-6050 on a joist/stud + DS18B20 (heating loads separate by their thermal
  signature).
- **Cooperation:** spectra identify *what*; temperature disambiguates the heating-related machines
  that look alike in vibration.
- **Mechanisms:** **F**, **C**, **D**.
- **Ground truth:** run each appliance on purpose and label it. A full labeled library in one
  evening, and cheap to re-record.
- **Resume line:** *"Whole-home appliance activity inference from a single structural vibration
  sensor: identified N appliances with X% accuracy from spectral fingerprints."*
- **Why it's unique:** the counterintuitive claim is the pitch — *one* sensor, nowhere near any of
  the machines, knowing what the whole house is doing.

## 7. Acoustic disdrometer — rainfall rate from individual drop impacts
- **The trick:** a piezo under a taut plate hears every raindrop, and *impact energy scales with
  drop size.* Counting and sizing drops gives you a drop-size distribution and a rainfall rate.
  Meteorological disdrometers cost $2,000+.
- **Sensors (~$5):** piezo disc on a plate + BMP280 (pressure/front context) + optional temp for
  rain-vs-sleet.
- **Cooperation:** impacts give intensity; pressure and temperature give the storm context that
  says whether you're seeing rain, sleet, or hail (hail impacts are enormous outliers).
- **Mechanisms:** **B** (impacts are asynchronous interrupts arriving in bursts — a genuine
  interrupt-storm stress test), **F**, **D**.
- **Ground truth:** a $10 tipping-bucket gauge or a straight-sided jar and a ruler; a garden hose
  on mist setting for controlled trials.
- **Resume line:** *"Acoustic disdrometer estimating rainfall rate from per-drop impact energy:
  within X% of a tipping-bucket reference across N events."*

## 8. Train-crossing predictor (very Fort Collins)
- **The trick:** an approaching train announces itself in the ground long before it arrives, and
  in the air (horn) at a known sequence. Fort Collins' downtown crossings block traffic for 10+
  minutes, and students plan around them badly.
- **Sensors (~$6):** piezo/geophone coupled to the ground near the track + microphone module
  (horn detection) + optional magnetometer (steel mass passing).
- **Cooperation:** seismic gives early warning and approach direction from amplitude trend;
  acoustic confirms and rejects a passing truck; together you get a *lead-time estimate*, which
  neither gives alone.
- **Mechanisms:** **F**, **C**, **D** + query CLI ("how often is this crossing blocked at 7:50
  a.m.?" — a past-tense question again).
- **Ground truth:** stand there with a stopwatch; the trains run on a schedule you can log.
- **Resume line:** *"Seismic-acoustic train detection with X seconds median advance warning and a
  blockage-duration history queryable by time of day."*
- **Catch:** **stay off railroad property** — this works from a public sidewalk or private
  property near the line, and the memo should say that explicitly.

## 9. Acoustic fixture disaggregation from one pipe clamp
- **The trick:** one piezo clamped to a main water line hears every fixture in the building, and
  arrival delay plus high-frequency attenuation encodes *distance* — so the upstairs bathroom
  sounds measurably different from the kitchen sink.
- **Sensors (~$6):** piezo on the pipe + DS18B20 on the hot line (hot vs cold draw).
- **Cooperation:** acoustic signature says which fixture; hot-line temperature response confirms
  whether hot water was drawn, resolving the fixtures that sound alike.
- **Mechanisms:** **F**, **C**, **D**.
- **Resume line:** *"Fixture-level water-use disaggregation from a single pipe-clamped contact
  microphone: N fixtures classified at X% accuracy using acoustic signature and thermal

  weeks). Also: presence detection — the bed knows when it's occupied, which gates everything.

After people leave a room, CO2 decays exponentially, and the decay constant **is** the room's air changes per hour. Ventilation engineers measure this with tracer gases and equipment costing thousands.

The reed switch on the door isn't a second data stream — it's the *validity condition* for the first one's analysis, which is a nice thing to be able to say in a design doc. Ground truth: breathe into the room, leave, fit the decay. Repeat with the door open, window open, fan on — four labeled conditions in an afternoon.

> *"Measured room air-change rates from CO2 decay-curve fits across N ventilation conditions, quantifying a Z× difference between closed-door and cracked-window states."*

## 6. One sensor, whole-house appliance census

Every machine couples vibration into the structure. A single accelerometer on a floor joist hears the furnace, washer, dryer, garage door, and footsteps — each with a distinct spectral fingerprint, all through the wood. ~$6.

The counterintuitive claim *is* the pitch: one sensor, nowhere near any of the machines, knowing what the whole house is doing.

> *"Whole-home appliance activity inference from a single structural vibration sensor: identified N appliances with X% accuracy from spectral fingerprints."*

## 7. Acoustic disdrometer

A piezo under a taut plate hears every raindrop, and **impact energy scales with drop size** — so you get a drop-size distribution and a rainfall rate. Meteorological disdrometers cost $2,000+. Yours is $5.

Mechanism B is a real stress test here: impacts arrive as asynchronous interrupt bursts. Ground truth: a jar and a ruler, or a garden hose on mist for controlled trials.

## 8. Train-crossing predictor

Very Fort Collins. An approaching train announces itself in the ground long before it arrives, and in the air by horn. Downtown crossings block traffic for 10+ minutes and students plan around them badly. Seismic gives early warning from the amplitude trend; acoustic confirms and rejects a passing truck; together you get a lead-time estimate neither gives alone. Plus a query CLI for the past-tense question: "how often is this crossing blocked at 7:50 a.m.?"

Stay off railroad property — this works from a sidewalk, and the memo should say so.

## 9. Fixture disaggregation from one pipe clamp

One piezo on a main water line hears every fixture in the building, and arrival delay plus high-frequency attenuation encodes *distance* — so the upstairs bathroom sounds measurably different from the kitchen sink. A hot-line temp probe resolves the fixtures that sound alike.

## 10. Hot-wire anemometer / heated-probe soil moisture

Heat a small resistor, measure how fast it cools. In air that gives airflow (commercial hot-wire anemometers: $200+). In soil it gives moisture, and unlike a capacitive probe it **doesn't corrode**. ~$5. The ambient reference probe is essential — the measurement is a differential — and the heat pulse must be precisely timed, so jitter is a direct error.

## 11. Tank level with no gauge

Liquid holds heat differently than the empty space above it. A vertical strip of temp sensors down the *outside* of a propane or water tank finds the discontinuity at the liquid line — no gauge, no drilling, no contact with the contents. RV and grill owners do this by hand with hot water; this automates it. Natural home for mechanism A (a multi-drop 1-Wire driver with real concurrent access).

## 12. Flash-flood / creek-stage early warning

A rangefinder over a culvert measures water stage; *rate of rise* plus rainfall gives lead time. Fort Collins has real flood history, and USGS gauges exist on rivers but not on the culvert behind your building. Rainfall with no stage response is itself a finding — the culvert is blocked.

---

## My ranking for uniqueness

1. **Sleep vitals from bed vibration** — heart rate through a mattress from a $5 load cell is the biggest "you did *what*?" here, and it's the only one you can validate against a reference instrument tonight.
2. **Flicker meter** — measures something nobody thinks to measure, against a real published standard, with a $500 commercial equivalent.
3. **Ultrasonic anemometer** — the cleanest physics-to-OS link anywhere in this file. Highest risk.
4. **Building envelope audit** — "I built the $400 energy audit for $8" is a great sentence, and it's the lowest-risk idea in the round.
5. **One-sensor house census** — the counterintuitive claim sells itself.

All twelve are in [brainstorm.md](Term%20Project/brainstorm.md) as Round 8, with the four uniqueness sub-patterns written at the top so you can generate more yourself. I also refreshed the project status in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) so a cold session knows which filters you've applied and what you've rejected.

# Round 9 (2026-09-22): STRICT 2-sensor builds, overestimated real-world pricing

Nick's correction: **exactly 2 sensors, no more** — not 3, and not "2 units of the same sensor
type" (that likely fails the spec's "physically distinct sensors" guardrail anyway — §3.1 almost
certainly means two different sensing modalities, not two copies of one part; play it safe).
Also: prior rounds used bulk/kit pricing ($1–4/sensor). That's unrealistic for single-unit
purchases. Below is repriced at **overestimated real single-unit retail** (rounded up, so actual
cost should come in under these numbers, not over).

## Overestimated single-unit sensor pricing (US retail, rounded up)

| Sensor | Modality | Overestimated price |
|---|---|---|
| DS18B20 waterproof temp probe | temperature | $8 |
| DHT22 | temp + humidity | $10 |
| BME280 | temp/humidity/pressure | $10 |
| HC-SR501 PIR | motion (passive IR) | $7 |
| HC-SR04 ultrasonic | range | $6 |
| MPU-6050 | vibration/accel | $8 |
| Reed/magnetic door switch | contact/position | $6 |
| HX711 + load cell | weight/force | $12 |
| Photoresistor (LDR) module | light | $6 |
| VL53L0X ToF | range (laser) | $12 |
| RCWL-0516 doppler | motion (through walls) | $7 |
| QMC5883L / HMC5883L magnetometer | magnetic field | $9 |
| Piezo disc + amp module | contact vibration/sound | $6 |
| KY-038 sound sensor module | sound (level, digital) | $7 |
| INMP441 I2S microphone | sound (streaming, analog-quality) | $9 |
| Rain-drop module | precipitation contact | $7 |
| Hall-effect flow sensor | liquid flow | $10 |
| IR break-beam pair (Adafruit-style) | beam interruption | $10 |
| MQ-7 CO sensor | gas | $9 |
| AS3935 lightning sensor | RF/electrical transient | $18 |
| MH-Z19 CO2 sensor | gas (NDIR) | $30 |
| MCP3008 ADC (needed for any analog sensor) | — (support chip, not a "sensor") | $9 |

**Pi rig, overestimated:**

| Item | Overestimated price |
|---|---|
| Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB), new | $65 |
| microSD card 32GB | $10 |
| Official power supply | $10 |
| Case + fan | $12 |
| Breadboard, jumper wires, resistors, misc | $12 |
| **Pi rig subtotal** | **$109** |

**So a realistic total, buying everything new and single-unit, is Pi rig ($109) + 2 sensors
(roughly $12–24 depending on choice) + an MCP3008 if either sensor is analog ($9) ≈ $130–150.**
That's well above the spec's stated $50–80/team, which assumes kit/bulk pricing or a used Pi.
**Ways to close the gap, all legitimate:** buy a used/older Pi (3B+ on eBay/FB Marketplace,
~$25–35), skip the case and fan (a project box or nothing works fine for a semester), buy sensors
from a multipack even if you only need one (often cheaper than a "single," you just have spares),
and check if CS370 or the CS department has a hardware loan/reimbursement program — ask before
assuming you're paying full retail out of pocket.

## Two-sensor project ideas (each exactly 2 distinct modalities)

1. **Freezer/fridge guardian, trimmed** — DS18B20 (inside) + reed switch (lid). ~$14. Drop the
   compressor accelerometer from earlier rounds; the two-sensor version still gets the core
   diagnosis (lid-open vs. slow-fail vs. sudden-fail) from temp trajectory shape alone, just with
   one fewer corroborating signal. Mechanisms D, E, B.
2. **Furnace short-cycle detector, trimmed** — MPU-6050 (blower vibration) + DS18B20 (supply-air
   temp). ~$16. Cycle segmentation from vibration; temperature rise per cycle says what the cycle
   achieved. Mechanisms F, C.
3. **Fermentation stall detector** — IR break-beam (bubble count) + DS18B20 (fermenter temp).
   ~$18. Temperature-compensated stall detection. Mechanisms B, D.
4. **Deadbolt watchdog** — 2 reeds is same-modality, so: reed (bolt state) + PIR (interior
   motion, for the learned-bedtime baseline). ~$13. Mechanisms B, D, E.
5. **Driveway vehicle ID** — magnetometer (signature) + PIR or reed (presence/gate trigger,
   confirms something is actually there rather than magnetic noise). ~$16 (+$9 MCP3008 if the
   magnetometer needs analog readout — check the specific breakout, many are I2C already).
   Mechanisms F/C, D.
6. **CO2-decay air-exchange rate** — MH-Z19 CO2 + reed switch (door state = validity condition
   for the decay-constant fit). ~$36. Priciest sensor pair here, but MH-Z19 is genuinely hard to
   substitute. Mechanisms E (UART sensor isolated in its own process), D.
7. **Flicker meter** — photoresistor/photodiode (light level, sampled fast via MCP3008) +
   DS18B20 (bulb housing temp, since driver flicker worsens with heat). ~$23 with the ADC.
   Mechanisms F, C.
8. **Whole-house structural census** — MPU-6050 (vibration) + DS18B20 (disambiguates
   heating-related machines that look similar in the vibration spectrum). ~$16. Mechanisms F, C.
9. **Acoustic disdrometer** — piezo (impact/drop count) + BME280 (pressure trend = storm
   context, also gives temp for rain-vs-sleet). ~$16. Mechanisms B, F.
10. **Package-porch log** — HC-SR04 or VL53L0X (range to drop zone) + PIR (presence/motion).
    ~$13–18. Mechanisms B, C.
11. **Explainable security node, trimmed** — PIR + HC-SR04 (range confirms size/distance, motion
    confirms it's not just wind). ~$13. Mechanisms B, C.
12. **Trash-can fill + raider** — HC-SR04/VL53L0X (fill level, inside lid) + PIR (outside,
    raccoon/bear at 3 a.m.). ~$13–18. Mechanisms C, B.
13. **Kitchen fan, trimmed to 2 sensors** — a gas/dust proxy (KY-038 sound module won't work for
    smoke; realistically this idea *needs* 3 modalities to work well — **flagging it as a poor
    fit for exactly 2 sensors**, listed here so you don't spend a week discovering that).
14. **Pipe-clamp fixture disaggregation, trimmed** — piezo (acoustic signature on the pipe) +
    DS18B20 (hot-line temp, confirms hot vs. cold draw). ~$14. Mechanisms F, C.
15. **Two-cat feeder, trimmed** — HX711 + load cell (mass, sampled fast enough for coarse gait) +
    IR break-beam (confirms a head actually entered the bowl opening, not just weight on the
    platform). ~$22. Mechanisms C, D.
16. **Sump-pump watchdog** — float switch/reed (interrupt on water level threshold) + MPU-6050
    (pump running vibration, distinguishes "ran and worked" from "never ran"). ~$14. Mechanisms
    B, F.
17. **Running-toilet detector, trimmed** — reed (flush handle) + DS18B20 on the supply pipe
    (flowing water chills it — this alone, without the SW-420 valve-vibration sensor, still
    catches "handle never moved but pipe stayed cold" = leak). ~$14. Mechanisms B, D.

**My pick under the strict 2-sensor + real-pricing constraint: #2, furnace short-cycle detector.**
Cheapest realistic total (~$16 sensors, and you likely have furnace access), F+C are forced by
the physics (a dropped vibration sample corrupts the cycle count; sampling jitter directly
distorts the spectrum), and the diagnosis genuinely needs both sensors — vibration alone can't
tell you if the cycle *achieved* anything, temperature alone can't tell you *why* it didn't.
Runner-up: **#5, driveway vehicle ID**, if you want the most unique story and have driveway
access — but confirm the magnetometer breakout's interface (I2C vs. analog) before buying, since
an analog one adds the $9 MCP3008 and a de-facto third component (still 2 *sensors*, one support
chip — worth stating that distinction explicitly in the design doc so it's not misread as a
third sensor).

## The 2-sensor constraint, and one thing worth flagging

"Physically distinct sensors" almost certainly means two different *modalities*, not two units of the same part — so all 17 below pair different sensor types. I trimmed several earlier 3-sensor ideas down to 2 and marked which ones actually survive the cut.
